title: Behavioral, mid data scientist, average answers

questions.text: Tell me about an analysis or model you owned from start to finish.
Tell me about a stakeholder who doubted your results.
Tell me about a model or analysis that turned out to be wrong.
Tell me about working with engineers to put a model into production.
Tell me about explaining results to a non-technical audience.
Tell me about a time you changed how your team works.

probe_areas: Mix of own work and team work

persona.pushback_style: asks what the candidate personally did

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Wen, thanks for joining. I'm Rafael, a data science lead. This is a thirty minute behavioral conversation.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Rafael, nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Did you have far to travel, or are you remote today?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Remote. I'm at home, so no travel.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Good. I'll ask about three or four past projects and leave a few minutes for your questions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about an analysis or model you owned from start to finish.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: At my last job I built a churn model for our subscription product. I pulled the data, built the features and trained a gradient boosting model. It got an AUC of 0.81 on the holdout set. The retention team used the top decile list for a campaign, and churn in that group fell by about 5 percent. I chose boosting over logistic regression because it was a bit more accurate, though it was harder to explain.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a model or analysis that turned out to be wrong.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We had a demand forecast that was off for a couple of months. The numbers did not match what sales saw. We looked into it and found some data issues, so we fixed the pipeline. It was a good lesson about checking data.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What was your part in finding it, and what did you change?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I found it. A source table had started double counting returns after a vendor update. I wrote a check that compares row counts every night, and it has caught two more problems since. I should have set up that monitoring from the start.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about working with engineers to put a model into production.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We worked with the platform team to deploy it. There were a lot of meetings about the API. Everyone was helpful and it went live in the end. I learned that communication matters.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What was the hardest part, and what did you decide?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The hard part was latency. The first version took 800 milliseconds and the product team wanted under 200. I proposed dropping two expensive features, which cost about 1 point of AUC. We hit 150 milliseconds and launched on time.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks. What questions do you have?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: What does the team's model review process look like?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Every model gets a written review with one reviewer outside the team, usually a week before launch.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's our time. Thanks Wen, you'll hear from the recruiter within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Rafael.

notes: Average for mid: one good story, two answers start generic and improve after a probe.
